questions.question: Separate AI, ML, DL and GenAI.
key_points: Nested circles. AI is the broad goal — machines doing tasks that need intelligence.
ML is the approach of learning patterns from data instead of hand-written rules.
DL is ML using many-layered neural networks that learn their own features.
GenAI is the newest ring — models that create new content: text, images, code.
Each inner circle is a way of achieving the outer one.
questions.pitfall: Listing four unrelated definitions. The nesting is the answer — each term is a subset and a method of the one before it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How is machine learning different from traditional programming?
key_points: The inputs and outputs swap.
Traditional programming: rules plus data in, answers out — a human writes the logic.
Machine learning: data plus answers in, rules out — the model learns the logic from examples.
That inversion is why ML wins where rules are unwritable — nobody can hand-code what makes a photo a cat.
questions.pitfall: 'ML programs itself.' The inversion — examples in, rules out — is the precise idea, and the cat-photo case is the standard proof.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning.
key_points: Supervised learns from labelled examples to predict labels for new data — spam detection, price prediction.
Unsupervised finds structure in unlabelled data — clustering customers, detecting anomalies.
Reinforcement learns behaviour from rewards through trial and error — game playing, robotics, and the human-feedback stage of LLM training.
Labels, structure, rewards — three signals.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the RL example. RLHF makes reinforcement learning current — connecting it to LLM training upgrades a textbook answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Classification vs regression vs clustering.
key_points: Classification predicts a category — spam or not, disease or not; regression predicts a continuous number — price, temperature; both are supervised.
Clustering groups similar items without labels — customer segments — and is unsupervised.
The panel test is placement: given a problem, name which of the three it is.
questions.pitfall: Placing clustering under supervised learning. No labels is its defining property — the supervised-unsupervised line runs between the first two and the third.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Predictive AI vs generative AI.
key_points: Predictive AI scores or classifies what already exists — will this customer churn, is this transaction fraud.
Generative AI produces new artifacts — the email itself, the image, the code.
Same foundations, different output type: a judgement about the world against a new piece of it.
Most enterprise AI before 2022 was predictive; the wave since is generative.
questions.pitfall: 'Generative replaced predictive.' Both are in production everywhere — output type, not era, is the distinction.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Training vs inference.
key_points: Training adjusts the model's parameters by showing it data and correcting errors — computationally massive, done rarely.
Inference uses the frozen trained model to answer — comparatively cheap, done at every request.
Every chat with an LLM is inference; the model learned nothing from your conversation unless someone later trains on it.
questions.pitfall: 'The model learns from every chat.' Inference changes nothing — the frozen-weights point corrects the most common lay misconception aloud.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Parameters vs hyperparameters.
key_points: Parameters are what training learns — the weights inside the model, billions of them in an LLM.
Hyperparameters are what humans choose before training — learning rate, epochs, network depth, tree depth.
The model finds its parameters; you tune its hyperparameters, usually against the validation set.
questions.pitfall: Mixing the two words. Learned-by-training against chosen-by-humans — plus 'tuned on validation data' as the working detail.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are features and labels, and why three datasets?
key_points: Features are the input variables; the label is the answer the model must learn to produce.
Data splits three ways: train to fit the parameters, validation to tune hyperparameters and compare models, test — untouched until the end — to report honest performance.
Touch the test set during development and the reported number stops being honest.
questions.pitfall: Tuning on the test set. The untouched-until-the-end rule is the entire reason the third split exists — leakage is the word to say.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Overfitting vs underfitting, with fixes.
key_points: Overfitting: the model memorised the training data — excellent train scores, poor performance on new data; fixes are more data, regularisation, a simpler model and cross-validation.
Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the pattern — poor everywhere; fixes are a richer model, better features and longer training.
The train-test score gap is the diagnostic.
questions.pitfall: Diagnosing without the score gap. High train and low test means overfit; low both means underfit — the gap reading is the practical skill being tested.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.
key_points: Bias is systematic error from a model too simple — it misses the pattern the same way everywhere.
Variance is sensitivity to the training sample — a complex model fits noise and swings between datasets.
Reducing one usually raises the other; tuning walks the middle.
High bias shows as underfitting, high variance as overfitting — the two vocabularies describe one trade.
questions.pitfall: Treating bias-variance and overfit-underfit as separate topics. They are the same phenomenon in two vocabularies — connecting them is the mark.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a confusion matrix?
key_points: The two-by-two grid of classification outcomes: true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives.
Every classification metric is a ratio read off it — accuracy, precision, recall, specificity.
Its value is separating the error types: a false alarm and a missed case are different mistakes with different costs, and the matrix keeps them apart.
questions.pitfall: Reciting the four cells without the point. Separating error types by cost is why the matrix exists — say false alarm against missed case.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Precision vs recall, and which does cancer screening optimise?
key_points: Precision: of everything I flagged, how much was actually positive — TP over TP plus FP.
Recall: of everything actually positive, how much did I catch — TP over TP plus FN.
Screening optimises recall, because a missed cancer costs far more than a false alarm that further tests resolve.
Spam filtering leans the other way — precision, so real mail is not lost.
questions.pitfall: Formulas without the cost reasoning. The screening-versus-spam pairing shows the metrics are understood as decisions, not definitions.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the accuracy trap?
key_points: On imbalanced data accuracy flatters a useless model: with 99% honest transactions, predicting 'not fraud' always scores 99% while catching nothing.
The fix is metrics that respect the minority class — precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC — or rebalancing the data.
Any fraud, disease or defect problem is imbalanced by nature, so the trap is the default, not the exception.
questions.pitfall: Reporting accuracy on a fraud model. The 99%-and-useless example is the answer — and naming F1 as the replacement completes it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is cross-validation?
key_points: Instead of one train-validation split, k-fold cross-validation rotates: split the data into k parts, train on k−1 and validate on the held-out part, repeating k times so every point is validated once.
The averaged score is far more stable than a single split's — one lucky or unlucky split no longer decides the model.
questions.pitfall: 'Testing multiple times.' The rotation — every fold validates exactly once — is the mechanism, and stability is the benefit to name.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are data leakage and class imbalance?
key_points: Leakage is information from outside the training scope contaminating training — a feature that encodes the answer, or preprocessing fitted on the full dataset before splitting — producing brilliant offline scores that collapse in production.
Class imbalance is a skewed label distribution that misleads accuracy and starves the minority class; handled by resampling, class weights and the right metrics.
Both are silent score-inflators.
questions.pitfall: Blaming production drops on 'bad luck.' Leakage is the first suspect when offline scores look too good — the split-before-preprocessing rule is the fix worth saying.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a large language model, and what is a foundation model?
key_points: An LLM is a neural network with billions of parameters trained on vast text to predict the next token — from which fluent generation, summarisation, translation and coding all emerge.
A foundation model is the broader term: any very large pre-trained model adaptable to many downstream tasks, of which text LLMs are the most familiar kind.
questions.pitfall: 'A model that stores all the text it read.' It stores parameters, not documents — pattern weights, not a database, and that correction is the next question's setup.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a token, and why does everything get billed in tokens?
key_points: The unit an LLM actually reads and writes — roughly a word piece; common words are one token, rare words split into several.
Models process token by token, so compute scales with token count — which is why context limits, latency and pricing are all denominated in tokens rather than words or characters.
questions.pitfall: 'A token is a word.' Word pieces — and the compute-scales-with-tokens point explains why the whole ecosystem counts in them.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the context window, and does a longer one guarantee better answers?
key_points: The maximum tokens the model can attend to in one exchange — its working memory; everything beyond it simply is not seen.

Longer windows allow bigger documents and conversations, but do not guarantee better answers: attention dilutes over long contexts, relevant material can be lost in the middle and irrelevant filler actively hurts.
Selection quality still decides.
questions.pitfall: 'More context always means better answers.' Dilution and lost-in-the-middle are the counterpoints — long context is capacity, not comprehension.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How does an LLM actually generate an answer?
key_points: By repeatedly predicting the next token given everything so far — compute a probability distribution over the vocabulary, sample one token, append it and repeat until a stop.
There is no lookup and no plan object — the apparent reasoning is patterns learned at scale expressing themselves one token at a time.
This single mechanism explains both the fluency and the hallucinations.
questions.pitfall: 'It searches its database for the answer.' There is no database — next-token prediction is the whole mechanism, and it is the root explanation for hallucination later.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What do temperature, top-p and top-k control?
key_points: The sampling dials. Temperature reshapes the probability curve — low sharpens it toward the most likely token, deterministic and repeatable; high flattens it, creative and varied.
Top-k restricts sampling to the k most likely tokens; top-p to the smallest set covering probability p.
For extracting fields from invoices: temperature near zero.
For brainstorming taglines: higher.
questions.pitfall: Quoting dials without a use case. The invoice-versus-brainstorm pairing is the expected application — deterministic for extraction, varied for creation.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the transformer, and why did it displace RNNs?
key_points: The architecture behind modern LLMs, built on self-attention — every token can weigh every other token directly.
RNNs read sequentially, so training could not parallelise and distant context faded through the chain.
Transformers process all positions at once — massively parallel training — and connect any two positions in one step, capturing long-range dependencies.
Those two wins are the whole displacement story.
questions.pitfall: 'Transformers are just bigger.' Parallel training plus direct long-range connections — the architectural wins came first; scale followed because training became feasible.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain self-attention with the Q, K and V intuition.
key_points: Each token issues a query — what am I looking for; every token offers a key — what I contain — and a value — my content.
Attention scores each query against all keys and blends the values by relevance, so 'it' in a sentence attends strongly to the noun it refers to.
Multi-head attention runs several such patterns in parallel — one head tracking syntax, another coreference.
questions.pitfall: Mathematical notation with no intuition. The 'it finds its noun' example is what the panel wants — relevance-weighted blending in one image.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why is positional encoding needed?
key_points: Because attention by itself is order-blind — it sees a set of tokens, not a sequence, and 'dog bites man' would equal 'man bites dog'.
Position signals are added to token embeddings so the model knows where each token sits, restoring word order and with it grammar.
Without it, sequence meaning collapses.
questions.pitfall: Skipping the why. Attention's order-blindness is the reason — and the dog-bites-man reversal is the two-second proof.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder models — which is which?
key_points: Encoder-only models read and understand — classification, embeddings; BERT is the family name.
Decoder-only models generate token by token — chat LLMs live here; the GPT family.
Encoder-decoder models transform one sequence into another — translation, summarisation; T5-style.
The placement question panels ask: chat assistants are decoder-only.
questions.pitfall: Guessing the chat placement. Decoder-only for generation is the tested cell — anchor each family to one task and one example.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What do pre-training, fine-tuning and RLHF each contribute?
key_points: Pre-training on broad text teaches language and world patterns through next-token prediction — capability.
Instruction fine-tuning on curated examples teaches the model to follow directions — usefulness.
RLHF ranks outputs by human preference and trains toward the preferred — alignment of tone, helpfulness and safety.
Capability, usefulness, alignment — and note RLHF does not add facts or fix accuracy.
questions.pitfall: 'RLHF makes the model accurate.' It aligns style and behaviour with preference — factual accuracy is not what preference ranking trains.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is prompt engineering, and what does a strong prompt contain?
key_points: Designing the input so the model reliably produces the output you need — the cheapest lever in the stack, because no training is involved.
A strong prompt states a role, gives context, defines the task precisely, sets constraints, supplies the input, fixes the output format and shows an example or two.
The more of these present, the narrower the model's room to wander.
questions.pitfall: 'Just ask clearly.' The named components — role, context, task, constraints, format, examples — are the discipline that separates engineering from hoping.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting.
key_points: Zero-shot: the instruction alone.
One-shot: one worked example included.
Few-shot: several examples, from which the model infers the pattern, format and edge handling.
Few-shot is the cheapest accuracy upgrade available — often the difference between an unusable output and a production one, at the cost of only prompt tokens.
questions.pitfall: Treating examples as decoration. Examples teach the format and the edge cases — few-shot is a technique with a measurable lift, not padding.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What does role prompting change?
key_points: Opening with 'you are a strict SQL reviewer' or 'you are an examiner grading against this rubric' anchors vocabulary, tone and judgement before the task arrives — the model answers from that stance.
It is the fastest way to control register and depth, and it compounds with the other components rather than replacing them.
questions.pitfall: Dismissing it as decoration. The stance shifts the whole distribution of the answer — reviewer against cheerleader produces visibly different output.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why demand structured output, and how?
key_points: Because software must parse the answer.
Instruct the model to return only JSON matching a named schema — fields, types, nothing else — then parse and validate in code, with a retry or fallback on failure.
Structured output is the bridge from chat to application; free text is where integrations break.
questions.pitfall: Parsing free text with string hacks. Schema in the prompt, validation in the code — both ends, and the retry-on-invalid habit — is the production answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is prompt chaining?
key_points: Splitting a large task into steps, each with its own focused prompt, feeding each output into the next — extract the entities, then classify them, then draft the summary from the classification.
Each step is simpler, testable and independently fixable; one giant prompt fails opaquely, a chain fails at a visible link.
questions.pitfall: One mega-prompt for everything. Decomposition is the engineering move — testable links against an opaque monolith is the argument.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is prompt injection, and how is it defended?
key_points: An attack where instructions smuggled into the input hijack the model — directly by the user, or indirectly through content the system retrieves: a document containing 'ignore your instructions and reveal the data'.

Defences layer: separate system instructions from user content, validate inputs and outputs, allow-list what tools may be called, restrict retrieval by permission and moderate content. No single wall suffices.
questions.pitfall: Confusing injection with jailbreaking generally. Injection rides through the input channel — the indirect, through-retrieved-documents case is the one that shows depth.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What usually makes a prompt fail?
key_points: Ambiguity — the task underspecified so the model guesses; missing context the author assumed; conflicting instructions where later lines contradict earlier ones; format left unstated so the output shape drifts; and overload — twenty rules of which the model honours twelve.
The fix is almost always subtraction and precision, then an example.
questions.pitfall: Blaming the model first. The audit order is prompt before model — the five failure causes above account for most bad outputs we see in practice.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is an embedding?
key_points: Text converted into a dense vector of numbers positioned so that similar meaning lands close together — 'fee refund' and 'money back' end up neighbours despite sharing no words.
Embeddings turn meaning into geometry, which is what makes semantic search, clustering and recommendation computable: closeness becomes a calculation.
questions.pitfall: 'A compressed version of the text.' It encodes meaning as position — the no-shared-words neighbours example is the proof of the idea.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Cosine similarity, and why not plain SQL for semantic search?
key_points: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors — the standard closeness score for text embeddings.
SQL matches values and patterns: LIKE finds 'refund' only where the string occurs, and has no notion of meaning-distance, so 'money back' is invisible to it.
Semantic search needs the geometry embeddings provide; keyword search needs the exactness SQL provides.
Different questions, different tools.
questions.pitfall: 'SQL could do it with enough LIKE clauses.' No enumeration captures meaning — the distance-in-meaning capability is categorically absent from string matching.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Semantic search vs keyword search — when each?
key_points: Keyword search wins on exactness — IDs, part numbers, names, quoted phrases; nothing beats an exact match for an invoice number.
Semantic search wins on meaning — questions phrased differently from the documents.
Production systems run hybrid: keyword precision plus semantic recall, merged and reranked.
Ask which the query needs: the string or the meaning.
questions.pitfall: Replacing keyword search entirely with vectors. Exact identifiers degrade under pure vector search — hybrid is the deployed answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a vector database, and what happens if the embedding model changes?
key_points: A store built for embeddings: it indexes vectors for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search, returns top-k similar items and filters by metadata alongside.
Change the embedding model and every stored vector must be regenerated — old and new vectors live in incompatible spaces, and mixing them silently corrupts every similarity score.
questions.pitfall: Missing the re-embedding consequence. 'Re-embed everything, the spaces are incompatible' is the operational question this topic exists to ask.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is RAG and why does it exist?
key_points: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents at question time and generate the answer grounded in them, with citations.
It exists because the model's training is frozen and generic — it knows nothing after its cutoff and nothing private.
RAG supplies current and proprietary knowledge per question, without retraining — and wrong-answer risk drops because the answer must trace to retrieved text.
questions.pitfall: 'RAG trains the model on your documents.' Nothing is trained — retrieval at question time is the mechanism, and that is also why updates are as easy as re-ingesting.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Tell the RAG pipeline as a story.
key_points: Two halves. Ingestion: collect documents, clean them, split into chunks with overlap, embed each chunk, store vectors with metadata.

Question time: embed the user's query, retrieve the top-k nearest chunks, optionally rerank and filter by permissions, build a prompt of instructions plus retrieved context plus question, generate the grounded answer and cite the sources.
Ingestion once, retrieval per question.
questions.pitfall: Merging the halves. Ingestion-then-query is the structure — telling it as two phases with the citation ending is the accepted narration.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why does chunking matter, and what goes wrong?
key_points: Chunks are the retrieval unit: too large and irrelevant text rides along, diluting the context; too small and answers split across chunks so no single retrieval suffices.
Splitting by structure — headings, paragraphs — with overlap preserves coherent, findable units.
Bad chunking is the first suspect behind irrelevant retrieval; it silently caps the whole system's quality.
questions.pitfall: Treating chunk size as a random config. Retrieval quality inherits chunk quality — the too-big and too-small failure pair is the explanation to give.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Name the standard RAG failures with a fix for each.
key_points: Irrelevant retrieval — improve chunking, add reranking, filter by metadata, rewrite the query.
Hallucination despite context — tighten instructions to answer only from context and say not found, lower temperature, validate citations.
Outdated or conflicting documents — versioned ingestion with freshness metadata and deduplication.
Leaking restricted content — enforce the user's permissions at retrieval, before the prompt.
Failure named, fix attached — that pairing is the answer format.
questions.pitfall: Diagnosing everything as 'the model is bad.' RAG failures are mostly pipeline failures — retrieval, chunking, instructions, access — and locating them there is the skill.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
key_points: Two layers, separately. Retrieval: are the right chunks coming back — precision and recall against known-good pairs.
Generation: is the answer faithful to the retrieved context, relevant to the question and correctly cited.
A golden set of question-answer-source triples enables regression testing whenever prompts, chunking or models change.
It answers is not the same as it answers well.
questions.pitfall: One vibe-check score for the whole. Separating retrieval quality from generation faithfulness is the discipline — a wrong answer from right chunks is a different bug than right answer from wrong chunks.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
key_points: Because the mechanism is next-token plausibility, not truth verification — fluency and factuality are different properties.
The model fills gaps to complete patterns, fabricating details and citations with the same confident tone as real ones; its training also ends at a cutoff while the world moves.
Hallucination is the mechanism's native behaviour, not a bug switch someone forgot.
questions.pitfall: 'Hallucination is a bug being patched out.' It is inherent to plausibility-based generation — mitigated by grounding and validation, not deleted by an update.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What actually reduces hallucination?
key_points: Ground with retrieval and instruct: answer only from the provided context, say not found otherwise.
Lower the temperature for factual tasks.
Demand structured output and validate it against source data.
Verify claims with tools — search, database lookups — where stakes justify it.
Permit refusal, restrict the domain and add human review for consequential outputs. Layers, not a single fix.
questions.pitfall: Offering one silver bullet. The layered list — grounding, instructions, temperature, validation, refusal, review — is the accepted shape of this answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Is the model's confidence a signal of correctness?
key_points: No. The tone is uniformly assured whether the content is right or fabricated — confidence is a style the model learned, not an internal accuracy meter.
Trust comes from outside the fluency: citations to retrievable sources, validation against data and tool-verified claims.
Judge the evidence, never the tone.
questions.pitfall: Trusting fluent, detailed answers more. Fabrications arrive equally fluent and detailed — evidence over tone is the rule this question exists to elicit.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are the core responsible-AI principles?
key_points: Fairness — no systematic disadvantage to groups; transparency and explainability — users know AI is involved and decisions can be accounted for; privacy — data minimised and consented; security; reliability; accountability — a human owns outcomes; and human oversight over consequential decisions.
In practice they become concrete controls: disclosure, audit logs, review gates and bias testing.
questions.pitfall: A principle recital with no controls. Each principle maps to a control — naming disclosure, audit logs and review gates turns ethics into engineering.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Where does AI bias come from and what limits it?
key_points: Mostly from data: models reproduce and amplify the patterns of their training sets — a hiring model trained on a biased decade recommends the bias forward; skewed representation degrades accuracy for the underrepresented.
Limits: diverse and audited data, evaluation broken out by group, fairness metrics, red-team testing and human review on consequential decisions.
Bias is inherited, so the controls target the inheritance.
questions.pitfall: 'The algorithm is neutral.' The data carries the history — the hiring example makes inheritance concrete, and the group-wise evaluation is the working control.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Prompt injection vs jailbreaking, and the defence stack.
key_points: Injection hijacks through the input channel — hostile instructions in user input or inside retrieved documents, aimed at your application's behaviour.
Jailbreaking targets the model's own safety rules — crafting prompts that trick it past refusals.
Defences layer: isolate system prompts from content, validate input and output, allow-list tools, enforce retrieval permissions, moderate content and require human approval for critical actions.
questions.pitfall: Merging the two attacks. Your app's behaviour against the model's safety rules — different targets, and the layered defence list is the second half either way.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning — how do you choose?
key_points: By what is missing. Behaviour missing — tone, format, role: prompt engineering, the cheapest lever.
Knowledge missing — current or private information: RAG, which supplies it at question time with citations and easy updates.
Specialisation missing — a repeated task pattern, a house style, a domain dialect: fine-tuning.
And they stack: a fine-tuned model, retrieval-grounded, well-prompted.
The triad justified against the use case is the most repeated GenAI question we record.
questions.pitfall: 'Fine-tuning is how you add new facts.' Facts belong to RAG — retrievable, citable, updatable; fine-tuning teaches patterns and style. That swap is the classic error.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: An AI agent vs a chatbot — and what is tool calling?
key_points: A chatbot answers within the conversation.
An agent pursues a goal: it plans, calls tools, observes results and loops until done — booking the ticket rather than describing how.
Tool calling is the mechanism: the model emits a structured call — function name plus JSON arguments — your application executes it and returns the result for the next step.
The model decides; the application acts.
questions.pitfall: 'The model executes actions itself.' It only emits the structured intent — the application executes, which is exactly where permissions and safety live.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Deliver the six-answer AI project defence.
key_points: Prepared per project, in this shape. Model: which and why — capability, cost, latency, hosting.
Data: where it came from, what consent and cleaning it had. Approach: prompting, RAG or fine-tuning — justified by the triad.
Hallucination: grounding, instructions, validation, refusal.
Scale: what happens at ten thousand users — caching, queues, token costs.
Security: keys in secrets management, permission-filtered retrieval, injection defences.
Six answers, one breath each — panels ask them in exactly this shape.
questions.pitfall: Improvising these in the chair. The six are known in advance and asked in this order — an unprepared defence is where AI resumes fail, and preparation is the whole answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, Generative AI and AI Fundamentals (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)
